# Pilonidal disease

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Emergency medicine > Gastrointestinal disorders > Pilonidal disease*

[Original Article Link](/library/Y30nSf)

---

## Summary

Pilonidal disease, caused by loose <u>hair</u> penetrating the <u>gluteal cleft</u> tissue, can manifest as acute <u>abscesses</u> or chronic cysts and sinuses with persistent drainage. Pilonidal disease is most common in young adult men. <u>Risk factors</u> include a deep <u>gluteal cleft</u>, excessive body <u>hair</u>, prolonged sitting, friction, and <u>PCOS</u>. Symptoms range from mild drainage and <u>erythema</u> to severe <u>pain</u> from <u>abscesses</u>. Chronic pilonidal disease involves recurrent infections and sinus tract discharge. Diagnosis is based on <u>patient history</u> and <u>clinical examination</u>. Treatment depends on severity, from <u>incision and drainage</u> for acute pilonidal <u>abscesses</u> to surgical interventions for chronic pilonidal disease.

---

## Epidemiology

* Sex: <u>♂</u> > <u>♀</u> (∼ 3:1)

* Peak <u>incidence</u>: 15–25 years [[1]](/library/hh0cdf)




Epidemiological data refers to the US, unless otherwise specified.

---

## Pathophysiology

The exact mechanism is unknown, however, the current prevailing hypothesis is that pilonidal disease is an acquired condition.




* Sitting or bending cause <u>hair follicles</u>, in vulnerable <u>skin</u> within a deep <u>gluteal cleft</u>, to stretch and break → formation of an open pore or pit. These open pores either collect debris or broken <u>hair</u> roots (from the head, back or buttocks).

* Movement causes negative pressure (e.g., “suction effect”) and further penetration of <u>hair</u> into local <u>subcutaneous tissue</u> → formation of a pilonidal sinus [[2]](/library/3h0Sdf)

* These collections trigger local tissue inflammation within the pilonidal sinus → acute infection (<u>abscess</u>) or <u>fistulae</u> [[3]](/library/Rh0ldf)[[4]](/library/ih0Jdf)

---

## Risk factors

* Excessive body <u>hair</u>

* <u>Obesity</u>

* Deep <u>gluteal cleft</u>

* Local irritation

* Sedentary lifestyle

* <u>Family history</u>

* <u>PCOS</u> [[7]](/library/QUdu160)

---

## Clinical features

* Pilonidal cyst: a cyst near the upper <u>gluteal cleft</u>, often containing <u>hair</u> and <u>skin</u> debris

* Acute pilonidal abscess: acute infection of a <u>pilonidal cyst</u>  

* <u>Pain</u>

* <u>Erythema</u>, <u>cellulitis</u>

* <u>Fluctuant</u> swelling <u>lateral</u> to midline

* <u>Purulent</u> discharge

* Possible <u>fever</u>

* Chronic pilonidal disease: presence of pits or persistent sinus tracts without acute <u>abscess</u> formation  

* May be asymptomatic or cause <u>chronic pain</u>

* Sinus openings (midline pits) may be visible superior (4–8 cm) to the <u>anus</u>.

* Drainage (<u>purulent</u>, mucoid, or blood‑stained) from sinus tracts

* Recurrent pilonidal disease: repeated episodes of acute infection

## Diagnosis

* Pilonidal disease is a <u>clinical diagnosis</u>. [[6]](/library/iUdJ160)[[9]](/library/6UdjV60)

* Examine the <u>gluteal cleft</u> for midline pits and sinus tracts.

* Evaluate for an <u>acute pilonidal abscess</u> and/or <u>cellulitis</u>, e.g., <u>soft tissue POCUS</u>

* Perform an anorectal examination to rule out <u>anorectal abscess and fistula</u>.

* Imaging (e.g., CT, US) is typically reserved for complex pilonidal disease to determine the extent of disease and rule out complications.





> [!TIP]
> Pilonidal <u>abscesses</u> are located near the upper <u>gluteal cleft</u>, whereas perirectal <u>abscesses</u> are located near the <u>anus</u>.

---

## Differential diagnoses

* <u>Anal fistula</u> (e.g., due to <u>Crohn disease</u>)

* <u>Hidradenitis suppurativa</u>

* <u>Anorectal abscess</u>

* <u>Sacrococcygeal teratoma</u>

* <u>Granulomas</u> (e.g., <u>syphilis</u>, <u>tuberculosis</u>)




The differential diagnoses listed here are not exhaustive.

---

## Treatment

### Approach [[5]](/library/xd1EHf0)[[6]](/library/iUdJ160)[[9]](/library/6UdjV60)




* All patients: lifestyle modifications to prevent recurrence

* Local hygiene

* <u>Hair</u> removal (e.g., laser epilation) [[10]](/library/kh0mVf)[[11]](/library/afdQk60)

* Avoidance of tight-fitting clothes and prolonged periods of sitting

* <u>Acute pilonidal abscess</u>: : <u>incision and drainage</u> with or without <u>antibiotic</u> treatment

* Chronic or recurrent pilonidal disease: definitive management with minimally invasive and/or surgical treatment





### <u>Acute pilonidal abscess</u> [[5]](/library/xd1EHf0)[[6]](/library/iUdJ160)[[9]](/library/6UdjV60)




* All patients

* <u>Manage acute pain</u> with <u>NSAIDs</u>.

* Encourage symptomatic management, e.g., <u>sitz baths</u>, warm compresses

* Consider <u>antibiotics</u>. (See “<u>Antibiotics for purulent SSTIs</u>.”)  [[9]](/library/6UdjV60)[[12]](/library/jUd_160)[[13]](/library/AN1Rdh0)

* Simple <u>abscess</u>: Perform <u>incision and drainage</u>.

* Avoid making an <u>incision</u> that crosses the midline.  [[8]](/library/3wYSir)

* Consider packing the wound to allow for <u>secondary wound closure</u>. [[14]](/library/Ev18bQ0)

* Refer to <u>surgery</u> for definitive <u>pilonidal cyst</u> management.

* Complicated <u>abscess</u> (e.g., deep, large, multiple sinus tracts): Consult <u>surgery</u>.





> [!WARNING]
> Do not perform <u>incision and drainage</u> in the absence of <u>fluctuance</u>: Premature <u>incision</u> before <u>abscess</u> formation may cause extension of the infectious process. [[8]](/library/3wYSir)




### Recurrent or chronic pilonidal disease [[5]](/library/xd1EHf0)[[6]](/library/iUdJ160)[[9]](/library/6UdjV60)




* Refer to <u>surgery</u> for definitive management.

* Treatment options include:

* Minimally invasive procedures, e.g., <u>phenol</u> or <u>fibrin</u> glue application to cyst and sinus tracts, sinusectomy

* Excision with <u>primary closure</u>, e.g., Karydakis <u>flap</u>, Bascom cleft-lift  [[15]](/library/PUdWW60)

* Excision with <u>secondary wound closure</u>, with or without <u>marsupialization</u>  [[16]](/library/JUdsV60)
